opus-5.5.text:
I think post-training is fundamentally about taste and intuition, and you can't really get that from reading papers alone. When someone spends a lot of time actually playing with models, chatting with them, poking at them, trying weird prompts, comparing different versions side by side, they develop a feel for what a model is good at, where it breaks, and what "good" even looks like. That sense is very hard to write down as a metric.

In pre-training, a lot of the signal is relatively clean. You watch the loss, you scale data and compute, and there are fairly well-understood laws. But in post-training, the objective is much fuzzier. You're shaping behavior, style, reasoning habits, how the model handles ambiguity, whether it's actually helpful or just looks helpful. Benchmarks only capture a small slice of that, and they can easily mislead you. So the people who do well are the ones who can look at a model's output and immediately sense, "this is off," or "this is a real improvement, not just a benchmark bump."

People who love playing with models also tend to be the ones who notice small things. They'll say, "Hey, the new checkpoint is a bit more verbose," or "it's started hedging on this kind of question," or "its reasoning got shorter but less careful." Those observations often turn into the next data recipe or the next reward design. A lot of progress in post-training comes from that loop: use the model, find the problem, figure out what data or training signal caused it, fix it, and use it again.

And honestly, curiosity matters a lot. If you genuinely enjoy talking to the model and exploring its boundaries, you'll do it without being asked, every day. That accumulated hands-on experience compounds. So when I look for people for post-training, I care less about whether someone has the perfect background on paper and more about whether they've really spent time with models and have their own opinions about them.

r001.rationale: The response says hands-on model use builds a feel for what models can do, where they break, and their boundaries.

r002.rationale: It connects finding problems to data recipes and reward design, but does not clearly state that discovering capability boundaries motivates seeking scalable ways to overcome them.

fable-5.1.text:
Because post-training is, at its heart, about taste. Pre-training is more like engineering: you have scaling laws, you have loss curves, you can look at a number and know roughly where you stand. Post-training is different. The loss going down tells you very little about whether the model actually became better to talk to, better at reasoning, better at following what a person really meant. The only reliable instrument we have for that is a human who has spent a lot of time with these models and has built up a feel for them.

People who play with models constantly develop something like intuition. They know what a model "sounds like" when it is confidently wrong. They notice when it over-hedges, when it is sycophantic, when it quietly drops a constraint in the prompt, when it gives a textbook answer instead of the answer the question needed. These are not things you find in a benchmark. You find them by poking at the model from a hundred angles, out of curiosity, often late at night, just because you want to see what happens.

That curiosity matters for a second reason. Post-training is a loop of hypothesis and verification. You think the model is weak on some kind of task, you construct data or a reward signal to fix it, you train, and then you have to check whether you actually fixed the thing or just taught the model to game your evaluation. Someone who enjoys interacting with the model will do that checking honestly and obsessively. Someone who only looks at aggregate metrics will miss that the model learned a shortcut.

And frankly, these people have good taste in data. If you have spent a long time asking models hard questions, you know what a good question looks like and what a good answer looks like. When you write SFT data or design preference pairs, that taste goes straight into the model. The model becomes a reflection of the judgment of the people who trained it, so you want people whose judgment was sharpened by actually using the thing.

So when I interview candidates, I care less about whether they have published on RLHF and more about whether they can sit down with a model and, within ten minutes, tell me three specific things that are wrong with it and why. That is the real skill. The algorithms you can learn in a few weeks. The taste takes much longer, and it only comes from playing.

r001.rationale: The response says people who play with models learn their weaknesses by probing them from many angles and can identify specific things that are wrong, communicating that hands-on experimentation reveals capability limits.

r002.rationale: It describes using data or reward signals and training to fix weaknesses, but does not say that discovering those limits motivates seeking scalable ways to overcome them.

astra-6.text:
I think post-training requires a very intuitive understanding of a model’s behavior. People who spend a lot of time playing with models notice things that a benchmark score might not capture: when an answer is technically correct but unhelpful, when the model misunderstands the user’s intent, or when a small change in the prompt produces a very different result.

That gives them a starting point for asking useful questions. Is this a capability the model lacks, or does it have the capability but fail to express it consistently? What kind of examples or feedback would help? Playing with models doesn’t replace the technical work, of course, but that curiosity and sensitivity to behavior can help you decide what to improve—and recognize whether you’ve actually improved it.

r001.rationale: The response says that playing with models reveals what they can do and where they fall short, including distinguishing a missing capability from inconsistent expression.

r002.rationale: It mentions asking what examples or feedback might help, but does not say that discovering capability limits motivates seeking scalable ways to overcome them.

sol-6.1.text:
I think post-training requires a very intuitive understanding of a model: what it’s good at, where it fails, and what kind of response actually feels useful. You develop that intuition by spending a lot of time using it, trying different prompts, and following up when something seems strange.

People who enjoy playing with models often notice things that a benchmark score doesn’t capture. A model might give a technically correct answer but miss what the user really wanted, or sound confident when it should ask a question. If you can recognize those differences and turn them into concrete examples, you have a good starting point for improving the model.

Of course, you still need rigorous experiments. But that curiosity helps you decide which experiments are worth doing.

r001.rationale: The response says that using models, trying different prompts, and following up on strange results builds intuition about what models do well and where they fail.

r002.rationale: It mentions turning observations into examples and choosing experiments, but does not say that discovering capability limits motivates finding scalable ways to overcome them.
